title: When Cholesterol Science Becomes Religion
description: If I take a step back and look at the state of cardiovascular medicine, I notice something conspicuous. We’ve invested decades of research and billions of dollars in the cholesterol hypothesis: the idea that high cholesterol—or, if we’re being more specific, LDL and ApoB-containing lipoprotein particles— causes cardiovascular disease. Therefore, the thinking goes, lowering these particles should reduce or even eliminate the disease. After all, if LDL is the central causal driver of atherosclerosis, then addressing them sufficiently should make the disease go away. That’s the simplistic narrative many of us are fed. And yet, we’ve been pursuing this model for half a century and have embarrassingly little to show for it. Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading killer. So, we should all be curious about what we obviously don’t understand. Right? However, I’ve also found that when you try to introduce nuance into this topic, it’s often treated not as valid scientific discourse, but as an ideological threat. Almost as if belief in the central importance of LDL cholesterol in cardiovascular disease is less a scientific model than a religion. And you don’t want to upset the priests. Let me begin to make my case with a short story, and then we’ll widen the lens to discuss a broader principle in medicine called the Overton Window, and why sometimes the moderate, reasonable point of view can look radical. A Cholesterol Question That Became Heresy Earlier this year, a paper was published in The New England Journal of Medicine —arguably the most influential medical journal in the world.

title: How to Lose Fat While Gaining Muscle (Proven by DEXA)
description: We used to think it was impossible to build muscle while losing fat—that you had to choose one or the other at any given point in time. I used to believe that myself. I was wrong. There’s nothing inherent in our biology that prevents us from doing both effectively at the same time. Let’s start with an example from our own StayCurious Metabolism community who, coincidentally, is actually named Nicholas N. Over the course of about a year and a half, he lost nearly half of his body fat, dropping almost 50 pounds of pure fat while gaining 25.6 pounds of muscle. No steroids or illicit compounds required. Now, that is certainly at the extreme end of the spectrum. But it proves an important point: it’s possible. And, to the point of this letter, it’s becoming easier and easier thanks to emerging tools. title: The Strange Science of Eating Only Meat
description: I ate over 100 pounds of meat in 30 days. And that’s not the craziest part. But before I tell you what happened we need context. The carnivore diet has had a fascinating trajectory over the past decade. It exploded into the mainstream as prominent advocates promoted it as a solution for everything from improving athletic performance and body composition to treating obesity, autoimmune disease, and other chronic illnesses. Recently, though, the narrative seems to have shifted. To many people, it looks like carnivore is on the decline. Part of that perception comes from some of its biggest public advocates moving away from strict carnivore. Perhaps the most notable example is Dr. Paul Saladino—better known as the Carnivore MD —who reintroduced fruit and other plant foods. So... did the carnivore diet fail? Did it simply follow the predictable life cycle of every fad diet? Is it fading away like a cauliflower fart in the wind? Not exactly. Because beneath the internet debates and social media hot takes is a much more nuanced story. And that’s what made me want to revisit the topic and re-try carnivore for myself. In fact, this wasn’t my first experience with carnivore. A few years ago, I followed the diet for five months, and overall, I had a surprisingly positive experience. Although, to be fair, my prior version was fairly liberal. I ate dairy, eggs, and... if I’m being honest... I also cheated with coffee. (Although I suppose if it had been kopi luwak, you could argue it was technically animal-based.) This time, though, I wanted to go further. More extreme. So, I went whole hog. Or perhaps, more appropriately... all cow. For 30 days, I followed the Lion Diet —the strictest version of carnivore. No dairy. No eggs. No seafood.
